report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Adolescents' expectancies and subjective task value beliefs for STEM decline across secondary school, yet few trials have compared different intervention components for enhancing these beliefs within the same trial.
This four-arm randomized trial, framed by situated expectancyvalue theory, compared brief online interventions focused around goal setting, role modeling, their combination, and an active control.
Participants were 855 Year 9 students (401 female, 454 male; M age = 14.68) across six Australian schools (3 urban, 3 rural).
Outcomes were expectancy, intrinsic value, utility value, and perceived cost for STEM overall and, in exploratory analyses, for biology, chemistry, and physics.
Compared to the control condition, the goal-setting-only condition produced higher post-intervention expectancy (Δ = 0.17, q = .034) and intrinsic value (Δ = 0.18, q = .034) but not utility value.
Role modeling alone produced no significant benefit after statistical correction.
The combined condition raised expectancy but also perceived cost.
No gender interaction was significant.

In rural (compared to urban) schools, exploratory analyses showed that, relative to the active control, goal setting alone raised utility value (Δ = 0.46, q < .001) and role modeling alone raised expectancy (Δ = 0.11, q < .001).

text.text: Exploratory subject-specific analyses showed similar goal-setting gains.
Results suggest that a brief, structured online goal-setting sequence can raise adolescents' immediate STEM expectancy and intrinsic value, warranting longer-term follow-up.

STEM participation builds the scientific and technical capabilities needed for innovation, productivity, and responses to challenges such as public health and environmental sustainability (Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2024), and demand for STEM-qualified workers in Australia continues to grow (Jobs and Skills Australia, 2024).

text.text: Whether students enter STEM pathways depends not only on capability but on whether they expect to succeed and see STEM as interesting, useful, and worth pursuing, beliefs that predict later subject choices, aspirations, and careers (Guo et al., 2015; Toh & Watt, 2022).

text.text: These changes occur shortly before Australian students confirm senior subject choices in Year 10, so supporting STEM motivation before then may broaden participation (Guo et al., 2015).

text.text: STEM participation is also uneven across students and educational contexts.

Female students remain substantially underrepresented in physics despite much stronger representation in biology (Australian Mathematical Sciences Institute, 2025; Marsh et al., 2019), a pattern consistent with evidence that stereotypes and identity-related beliefs shape how students evaluate different pathways within STEM (Cheryan et al., 2017).

text.text: Students in rural areas also encounter narrower senior-subject offerings, less access to specialist teachers, and fewer visible examples of STEM careers than their urban peers (Holden & Zhang, 2024), which may further narrow their participation in STEM.

text.text: Brief psychosocial interventions offer one way to strengthen STEM motivation.

Rather than changing curriculum content, they target students' beliefs, values, and interpretations of their academic experiences (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020; Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018), and they have produced favorable effects on interest, achievement, persistence, and course-taking (Brisson et al., 2017; Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009).

text.text: Despite these encouraging findings, three limitations constrain what this evidence can say about adolescents approaching consequential STEM choices (Rosenzweig & Wigfield, 2016).
text.formatted: Despite these encouraging findings, three limitations constrain what this evidence can say about adolescents approaching consequential STEM choices <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Rosenzweig & Wigfield, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: First, the strongest evidence comes from U.S. undergraduate courses (Asher et al., 2023; Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018), and school-based trials have targeted a single subject, typically mathematics (Brisson et al., 2017; Gaspard et al., 2015).

text.text: It remains unknown whether a brief intervention can shift beliefs about STEM as a broader domain, and whether effects are shared across biology, chemistry, and physics, which differ markedly in participation and gender composition.

Second, interventions are usually evaluated as complete packages and rarely compared with each component delivered alone, so which components move which beliefs, and whether combining components within a fixed session adds benefit or dilutes an otherwise effective component, cannot be determined (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018; Linnenbrink-Garcia et al., 2026).

text.text: Third, most school trials, unlike many college trials that randomize individual students online, randomize intact classrooms and deliver activities in person, so whether such activities retain their effects when delivered online, in a standardized format, within one scheduled class session is untested.
The present study addressed all three gaps.

Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) explains achievement-related choices in terms of students' beliefs about whether they can succeed and the value they attach to particular activities, extending the original expectancy-value model (Eccles et al., 1983).
text.formatted: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) explains achievement-related choices in terms of students' beliefs about whether they can succeed and the value they attach to particular activities, extending the original expectancy-value model <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Eccles et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Expectancy refers to students' beliefs about their likelihood of succeeding in a domain.

Subjective task value includes intrinsic value, or the interest and enjoyment derived from an activity; utility value, or its usefulness for future goals; attainment value, or its importance to the self; and perceived cost, or perceptions of what someone must give up to do a task, including the effort, opportunity costs, and emotional demands associated with participation (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020; Flake et al., 2015).

text.text: These beliefs are examined separately, as an intervention may change some and not others, and cost is not simply the inverse of positive value (Flake et al., 2015).

text.text: Under the "situated" view, these beliefs are shaped by students' experiences, social contexts, and interpretations of particular domains (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020), so brief interventions are more likely to shift immediate appraisals than enduring dispositions, and those appraisals may differ across STEM overall, biology, chemistry, and physics, and by gender and school setting.

text.text: Goal setting provides a structured way for students to translate broad aspirations into concrete and attainable actions.
Goal-setting theory proposes that specific goals can direct attention, mobilize effort, and promote strategy use more effectively than vague intentions (Locke & Latham, 2002).
text.formatted: Goal-setting theory proposes that specific goals can direct attention, mobilize effort, and promote strategy use more effectively than vague intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Locke & Latham, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In educational settings, proximal and attainable goals have been shown to support students' self-efficacy, achievement (Bandura & Schunk, 1981), and academic performance (Morisano et al., 2010), and implementation intentions can strengthen goal pursuit by specifying how students will respond when opportunities or obstacles arise (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006).
text.formatted: In educational settings, proximal and attainable goals have been shown to support students' self-efficacy, achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bandura & Schunk, 1981)</ref>, and academic performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Morisano et al., 2010)</ref>, and implementation intentions can strengthen goal pursuit by specifying how students will respond when opportunities or obstacles arise <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Personal-best goal setting likewise supports science aspirations (Martin et al., 2014) and problem solving (Ginns et al., 2018), though through repeated goals rather than a single brief activity.

text.text: The present study adapted these principles to a brief STEM-focused intervention that could be completed within one class session.

Students first reflected on the relevance of STEM to their own lives (a prompt drawn from utility-value interventions; Hulleman et al., 2010), then constructed a SMART goal (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound), evaluated whether the goal was achievable, identified strategies for dealing with distraction and difficulty, and formulated an implementation-intention plan.

text.text: Brief interventions integrating these elements have rarely been examined in secondary-school STEM with motivation as the immediate outcome.
Within SEVT, constructing an attainable goal and appraising whether it can be achieved may strengthen expectancy (Bandura & Schunk, 1981).
text.formatted: Within SEVT, constructing an attainable goal and appraising whether it can be achieved may strengthen expectancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bandura & Schunk, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: A goal may also strengthen utility value if it helps students connect STEM to their lives and futures (Hulleman et al., 2010).

text.text: Framing a self-generated goal around confidence, usefulness, or enjoyment may support intrinsic value (Locke & Latham, 2002; Martin et al., 2014).

text.text: Cost could move in either direction, as planning for difficulty and distraction may reduce perceived barriers (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006), whereas appraising the effort a goal requires may make those demands more salient.

text.text: Role models are people whose success shows others what is possible and how to achieve it (Morgenroth et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Role models are people whose success shows others what is possible and how to achieve it <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Morgenroth et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: They can shape students' motivation by providing concrete examples of people who have succeeded in domains that students may consider for themselves (Bandura, 1977; Dasgupta, 2011; Morgenroth et al., 2015).

text.text: In STEM, where stereotypes about who belongs, who can succeed, and who is interested in STEM (Master et al., 2016) shape self-concepts and aspirations, counter-stereotypical models may strengthen identification with the field (Dasgupta, 2011).

text.text: Exposure to women in STEM has been associated with stronger STEM self-concept and identification among female students (Stout et al., 2011), and brief role-model interventions have produced positive motivational effects in some studies (Buckley et al., 2022; González-Pérez et al., 2020).

text.text: Intervention effects may vary by gender, as female students often report lower expectancy and higher perceived cost in some STEM fields despite comparable achievement (Marsh et al., 2019; Watt et al., 2012).

text.text: Female STEM role models may be particularly motivating for female students when perceived similarity strengthens identification (Dasgupta, 2011; Stout et al., 2011), although stereotypical or psychologically distant models can have unintended negative effects (Cheryan et al., 2011).

text.text: Accordingly, both components were expected to benefit female students more than male students.
School location may also moderate effects.
The narrower STEM opportunities in rural settings noted above may shape how useful and attainable STEM appears to rural students.

Where pathways to STEM careers are less visible, rural students have fewer chances to consider what a STEM future could look like for them, so goal setting may strengthen the perceived usefulness of STEM for personal goals (Hulleman et al., 2010), and role models may make possible futures more visible and attainable (Morgenroth et al., 2015; Sjaastad, 2012).

text.text: With little prior evidence, location was examined as an exploratory moderator.

The present study tested whether two brief online activities, goal setting (GS) and role modeling (RM), could shift Year 9 students' expectancy, intrinsic value, utility value, and perceived cost for STEM.
Students were individually randomized within classes to one of four conditions in a 2 × 2 factorial design (GS only, RM only, combined GS + RM, or active control).
Within one scheduled class session, students completed a baseline survey (T1), their assigned intervention, and an immediate posttest survey (T2).

As the two activities target different SEVT processes, combining them was expected to offer a stronger option, delivering both approaches in one session (Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018; Linnenbrink-Garcia et al., 2026).
text.formatted: As the two activities target different SEVT processes, combining them was expected to offer a stronger option, delivering both approaches in one session <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Harackiewicz & Priniski, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Linnenbrink-Garcia et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Within a fixed session, however, combining them reduces the dose of each, so the combined condition tested whether they add value under a realistic time constraint.

The study asked whether the two components, alone or combined, improved students' overall STEM motivation (RQ1), whether their effects differed by gender (RQ2), and whether they differed by school location (RQ3).
Gender moderation was predicted, whereas location was examined without a directional prediction.
More adaptive motivation was defined as higher expectancy, intrinsic value, and utility value and lower perceived cost.
H1 and H2 addressed RQ1 and H3 addressed RQ2, whereas RQ3 and the subject-specific analyses were exploratory (Table S1).
text.formatted: H1 and H2 addressed RQ1 and H3 addressed RQ2, whereas RQ3 and the subject-specific analyses were exploratory (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: H1 (components).
text.formatted: H1 <ref type="bibr">(components)</ref>.

text.text: Students in conditions containing GS, and students in conditions containing RM, will report more adaptive overall STEM motivation (higher expectancy, intrinsic value, and utility value, and lower cost) than students in conditions without that component.
H2 (conditions vs. control).
Students in each intervention condition (GS only, RM only, and combined) will report more adaptive overall STEM motivation than students in the active control.
H3 (gender).
The benefits of GS and of RM will be larger for female than for male students.
Where this moderation is observed, the H2 contrasts will be examined separately for female and male students.

text.text: Participants were 865 Year 9 students randomized in six secondary schools (3 urban, 3 rural) in Victoria, Australia; the 855 analyzed students were 401 female and 454 male (M age = 14.68 years, SD = 0.55).
Ten students who reported a nonbinary gender identity were excluded (Section 2.8), so the primary analysis is a modified intention-to-treat analysis.
Participant flow follows the CONSORT guideline (Schulz et al., 2010; Figure S1), which also gives sample sizes by condition.
text.formatted: Participant flow follows the CONSORT guideline <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Schulz et al., 2010</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1</ref>), which also gives sample sizes by condition.

text.text: An a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007) targeted approximately 200 students per condition, providing 80% power to detect medium effects at α = .05.
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis in G*Power <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Faul et al., 2007</ref>) targeted approximately 200 students per condition, providing 80% power to detect medium effects at α = .05.

text.text: The schools were non-government (Catholic and independent), three rural (n = 480) and three urban (n = 375), and all had Index of Community Socio-Educational Advantage values above the national mean of 1,000 (Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, 2025).
In the Australian context, rural refers here to schools in regional Victoria and urban to schools in metropolitan Melbourne.
All students were taking compulsory Year 9 science.
The study was approved by a university Human Research Ethics Committee.
Data were collected between July and August 2025 using REDCap during a single scheduled class session.
Parents provided consent through each school's online consent platform, and students provided assent before participation.

Students first completed demographic questions and the baseline (T1) survey and were then individually randomized with REDCap's randomization module, using an unblocked allocation table generated by computer script before data collection; research staff could not view the table or anticipate the next allocation.
Students and teachers were not informed of condition assignments.
Allocation was unrestricted, and arm sizes ranged from 185 to 251, χ²(3) = 11.35, p = .010, although baseline means on all dependent measures were similar across conditions (Table 1).

text.text: Students then completed their assigned condition's online content and, immediately afterward, completed the posttest (T2) survey.
Each condition was scheduled for 35 minutes and included access to an interactive condition-specific chatbot (GPT-4o; Tables S2 and S3).

Students who missed the scheduled session (e.g., through excursions, illness, or technical difficulties) completed the same sequence when they next attended and were randomized the same way.

text.text: The factorial goal-setting effects on expectancy and intrinsic value remained significant after correction, and the utility-value effect remained nonsignificant.
As in the primary analysis, only the combined condition showed higher perceived cost than the active control (q = .032).
The GS-only contrasts on expectancy and intrinsic value were as large as in the primary analysis (Δ = 0.19 and 0.20 vs.
0.17 and 0.18) but no longer survived correction (q = .063), consistent with the loss of power from a sample one third smaller.
This study asked whether a brief online intervention could shift adolescents' STEM expectancy, values, and cost, and which component was responsible.
Goal setting raised expectancy and intrinsic value, both in the factorial analyses and in the direct comparison of goal setting alone with an active control.
Similarly, in the exploratory subject analyses, goal setting raised expectancy in biology and chemistry and intrinsic value in biology and physics.

Utility value did not change on average in any subject or overall, although exploratory analyses suggested that goal setting raised it in the rural schools, and that role modeling alone raised expectancy there.

Brief role-model videos produced no reliable average benefit, the combined condition added no benefit beyond the average of the two single-component conditions, and the registered gender interactions were not supported.
The goal-setting sequence may have made future engagement both more meaningful and more actionable, as students connected STEM to their lives, appraised a specific goal, and planned how to pursue it.

Appraising one's capability to reach an attainable goal may strengthen expectancy by making progress seem manageable (Bandura & Schunk, 1981), and generating a personally relevant goal may support intrinsic value through ownership of the activity (Koestner et al., 2008; Locke & Latham, 2002; Martin et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Appraising one's capability to reach an attainable goal may strengthen expectancy by making progress seem manageable <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bandura & Schunk, 1981)</ref>, and generating a personally relevant goal may support intrinsic value through ownership of the activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Koestner et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Locke & Latham, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Martin et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These findings extend SEVT-based intervention research, which has mostly targeted utility value through relevance writing (Hulleman & Harackiewicz, 2009), by showing that a single goal-setting session can shift expectancy and intrinsic value.

text.text: Because SEVT treats these beliefs as situated, such immediate shifts are a plausible first step toward later STEM choices.
Goal setting did not significantly raise utility value on average.
Its estimates were about as large as those for expectancy and intrinsic value but much less precise, so the average effect on utility value is uncertain rather than absent.
The exploratory location analyses offer one explanation.
Goal setting alone raised utility value markedly in the rural but not the urban schools, and this rural advantage appeared in each of biology, chemistry, and physics.
Students in rural settings, with narrower senior STEM offerings and fewer visible pathways (Holden & Zhang, 2024), may have had more to gain from connecting STEM to their own goals.
text.formatted: Students in rural settings, with narrower senior STEM offerings and fewer visible pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Holden & Zhang, 2024)</ref>, may have had more to gain from connecting STEM to their own goals.

text.text: Access to STEM opportunities was not measured, however, so this difference should be treated as a lead for replication rather than as an established rural-urban effect.
The utility-value factor also combined usefulness with general importance, so the design cannot separate a change in perceived usefulness from broader valuing of STEM.
Neither the role-modeling component nor the role-modeling-only condition improved any STEM-overall outcome.

Brief exposure to assigned role models may be insufficient to shift motivation for current STEM learning, particularly as role models are most influential when seen as relevant, relatable, and attainable (Morgenroth et al., 2015), perceptions that exposure alone may not foster and that were not assessed here.

text.text: One exploratory finding is a possible exception.

In the rural but not the urban schools, the role-modeling-only condition raised STEM expectancy relative to the active control, consistent with evidence that a relevant model's success can strengthen beliefs that success is attainable (Bandura, 1977), particularly for students with little exposure to STEM professionals (Sjaastad, 2012).

text.text: However, the factorial role-modeling effect did not differ by location, and location was confounded with school, so this finding warrants caution.
Future studies could test more personalized or repeated role-model exposure and measure similarity, identification, and attainability as mechanisms.

Delivering both components within one fixed session required reducing the dose of each, so the combined condition included three of the five role-model videos and a goal-setting sequence without the attainability appraisal, strategy selection, and implementation-intention plan.

It raised expectancy relative to the active control, so the abbreviated package retained some benefit, but its estimated gains were smaller than those of goal setting alone and no larger than the average of the two single-component conditions.
The design therefore cannot tell whether role modeling added little or abbreviating goal setting weakened an effective component.
The combined condition was also the only condition in which perceived cost was significantly higher than in the active control.

One explanation is that the abbreviated sequence omitted strategy selection and implementation planning, the elements most directly aimed at managing difficulty and distraction, so students may have registered the demands of STEM without a plan for meeting them.
Cost-focused interventions have similarly raised perceived cost at times when they made students' challenges and competing demands salient (Rosenzweig et al., 2022).

text.text: The factorial goal-setting estimate pointed in the same direction, but the goal-settingonly contrast was imprecise and not significant, so whether the full sequence also raises perceived cost remains open.
Contrary to the registered hypotheses, neither intervention component showed significantly greater benefits for female than male students on the primary STEM-overall outcomes.

In exploratory arm-level contrasts, goal setting alone raised female, but not male, students' intrinsic and utility value for chemistry, suggesting that a brief goal-setting activity may help female students find chemistry more interesting and useful, although the corresponding factorial interactions did not survive correction and replication is needed.

The prediction of greater benefits for female students was most direct for role modeling, given that all featured role models were women and similarity is central to role-model theory (Morgenroth et al., 2015), yet role modeling showed no gender moderation, suggesting that exposure to female exemplars alone may not be sufficient to produce stronger benefits for female students, particularly if the models were not also seen as attainable and similar, conditions without which role models can backfire (Cheryan et al., 2011).

text.text: Previous studies have mostly examined female role models in female or predominantly female samples (González-Pérez et al., 2020; Stout et al., 2011), leaving their comparative effectiveness across genders less well understood.

text.text: For schools, a brief online goal-setting intervention is a promising, low-cost way to strengthen students' STEM confidence and interest within one scheduled class session.
Where only one session is available, the full goal-setting sequence appears a better use of it than an abbreviated combination with role-model videos.

Before wider use, completion under routine delivery and the persistence of gains beyond the immediate posttest need to be established, and perceived cost should be monitored, particularly when goal setting is combined with other components.
If the rural findings replicate, goal setting and role-model videos may be most useful in schools where STEM pathways are less visible.
First, although randomization was at the student level and school-level ICCs were small, the trial included only six schools, so the rural-urban differences need replication in more schools.
Second, posttest retention differed across conditions and was lowest in the goal-settingonly condition, where a video fault stopped some students progressing.

FIML assumes that missingness is ignorable given the model variables; the complete-case analysis reproduced the primary pattern with similar effect sizes, but selection on unobserved characteristics cannot be ruled out.

Third, outcomes were self-reported immediately after a single exposure, minutes after students had rated their goal confidence or the role-model careers, so demand characteristics and short-term reactivity cannot be ruled out.
Immediate appraisals suit a brief intervention under SEVT, but whether they persist and shape later subject choices remains to be established.
Fourth, each condition was designed from prior work and tested as a package.

The goalsetting sequence combined a relevance reflection, capability appraisal, and implementation planning, each of which has produced benefits on its own (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006; Hulleman et al., 2010), so the design cannot identify which element carried the effect, and a dismantling design is needed to isolate its active ingredients.
text.formatted: The goalsetting sequence combined a relevance reflection, capability appraisal, and implementation planning, each of which has produced benefits on its own <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hulleman et al., 2010)</ref>, so the design cannot identify which element carried the effect, and a dismantling design is needed to isolate its active ingredients.

text.text: Although manipulation checks and minimum viewing times were in place, students' engagement with the content could not be measured directly, so weaker effects, particularly for role modeling, may partly reflect limited engagement.

A brief, structured online goal-setting intervention raised adolescents' immediate STEM expectancy and intrinsic value, whereas brief role-model videos did not, and combining the two within a fixed session did no better than the average of its parts.
Effects did not differ by gender on the main outcomes, although goal setting alone raised female students' intrinsic and utility value for chemistry in exploratory analyses.
Exploratory rural benefits of goal setting for utility value and of role modeling for expectancy need replication, as does the persistence of these gains into senior subject choices.
